claim: Depolarization of skeletal muscle resting potential contributes to failure of ECC in periodic paralysis.
source: Depolarization of skeletal muscle resting potential contributes to failure of ECC in diseases such as periodic paralysis, intensive care unit acquired weakness and possibly fatigue of muscle during vigorous exercise.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon in disease contexts.

claim: Depolarization of skeletal muscle resting potential contributes to failure of ECC in intensive care unit acquired weakness.
source: Depolarization of skeletal muscle resting potential contributes to failure of ECC in diseases such as periodic paralysis, intensive care unit acquired weakness and possibly fatigue of muscle during vigorous exercise.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon in disease contexts.

claim: Depolarization of skeletal muscle resting potential possibly contributes to fatigue of muscle during vigorous exercise.
source: Depolarization of skeletal muscle resting potential contributes to failure of ECC in diseases such as periodic paralysis, intensive care unit acquired weakness and possibly fatigue of muscle during vigorous exercise.
evidence: The use of 'possibly' indicates this is speculative.

claim: When extracellular K+ is raised to depolarize the resting potential, failure of ECC occurs suddenly over a narrow range of resting potentials.
source: When extracellular K+ is raised to depolarize the resting potential, failure of ECC occurs suddenly, over a narrow range of resting potentials.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Failure to generate Ca2+ transients occurs when APs peaked at potentials more negative than –30mV.
source: Simultaneous imaging of Ca2+ transients and recording of action potentials (APs) demonstrated failure to generate Ca2+ transients when APs peaked at potentials more negative than –30mV.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The integral of AP voltage with respect to time closely correlated with failure of the Ca2+ transient.
source: An AP property that closely correlated with failure of the Ca2+ transient was the integral of AP voltage with respect to time.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: AP conduction fails when APs peak below –21mV.
source: Simultaneous recording of Ca2+ transients and APs with electrodes separated by 1.6mm revealed AP conduction fails when APs peak below –21mV.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding stated in the abstract.

claim: AP conduction is governed by AP peak.
source: We hypothesize propagation of APs and generation of Ca2+ transients are governed by distinct AP properties: AP conduction is governed by AP peak, whereas Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum is governed by AP integral.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum is governed by AP integral.
source: We hypothesize propagation of APs and generation of Ca2+ transients are governed by distinct AP properties: AP conduction is governed by AP peak, whereas Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum is governed by AP integral.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Na channels have rapid kinetics and are insensitive to AP width.
source: Na channels, which govern propagation, have rapid kinetics and are insensitive to AP width (and thus AP integral) whereas Ca2+ release is governed by gating charge movement of Cav1.1 channels, which have slower kinetics such that Ca2+ release is sensitive to AP integral.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Cav1.1 channels have slower kinetics such that Ca2+ release is sensitive to AP integral.
source: Na channels, which govern propagation, have rapid kinetics and are insensitive to AP width (and thus AP integral) whereas Ca2+ release is governed by gating charge movement of Cav1.1 channels, which have slower kinetics such that Ca2+ release is sensitive to AP integral.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Depolarization in the t-tubules activates Cav1.1 channels.
source: Depolarization in the t-tubules activates Cav1.1 channels, which triggers opening of ryanodine receptors, Ca2+ exit from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), and force production (Melzer et al., 1995; Dulhunty, 2006; Bannister and Beam, 2013; Hernández-Ochoa and Schneider, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Activation of Cav1.1 channels triggers opening of ryanodine receptors.
source: Depolarization in the t-tubules activates Cav1.1 channels, which triggers opening of ryanodine receptors, Ca2+ exit from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), and force production (Melzer et al., 1995; Dulhunty, 2006; Bannister and Beam, 2013; Hernández-Ochoa and Schneider, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Opening of ryanodine receptors leads to Ca2+ exit from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
source: Depolarization in the t-tubules activates Cav1.1 channels, which triggers opening of ryanodine receptors, Ca2+ exit from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), and force production (Melzer et al., 1995; Dulhunty, 2006; Bannister and Beam, 2013; Hernández-Ochoa and Schneider, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Ca2+ exit from the sarcoplasmic reticulum leads to force production.
source: Depolarization in the t-tubules activates Cav1.1 channels, which triggers opening of ryanodine receptors, Ca2+ exit from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), and force production (Melzer et al., 1995; Dulhunty, 2006; Bannister and Beam, 2013; Hernández-Ochoa and Schneider, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Depolarization of the resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle causes failure of ECC in periodic paralysis.
source: Depolarization of the resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle, when severe enough, causes failure of ECC in diseases such as periodic paralysis and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired weakness (Lehmann-Horn et al., 2008; Cannon, 2015; Friedrich et al., 2015) as well as potentially contributing to fatigue during intense exercise (Allen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Depolarization of the resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle causes failure of ECC in ICU-acquired weakness.
source: Depolarization of the resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle, when severe enough, causes failure of ECC in diseases such as periodic paralysis and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired weakness (Lehmann-Horn et al., 2008; Cannon, 2015; Friedrich et al., 2015) as well as potentially contributing to fatigue during intense exercise (Allen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Depolarization of the resting membrane potential potentially contributes to fatigue during intense exercise.
source: Depolarization of the resting membrane potential of skeletal muscle, when severe enough, causes failure of ECC in diseases such as periodic paralysis and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired weakness (Lehmann-Horn et al., 2008; Cannon, 2015; Friedrich et al., 2015) as well as potentially contributing to fatigue during intense exercise (Allen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and the use of 'potentially' indicates speculation.

claim: Whole muscle force is generally stable or slightly increased with mild depolarization of the resting potential in frog and mammalian skeletal muscle.
source: Studies of depolarization-induced failure of ECC in frog and mammalian skeletal muscle reveal that whole muscle force is generally stable or slightly increased with mild depolarization of the resting potential, followed by a steep decline with further depolarization by only a few mV (Holmberg and Waldeck, 1980; Renaud and Light, 1992; Cairns et al., 1997; Yensen et al., 2002; Cairns et al., 2011; Pedersen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Whole muscle force shows a steep decline with further depolarization by only a few mV after mild depolarization.
source: Studies of depolarization-induced failure of ECC in frog and mammalian skeletal muscle reveal that whole muscle force is generally stable or slightly increased with mild depolarization of the resting potential, followed by a steep decline with further depolarization by only a few mV (Holmberg and Waldeck, 1980; Renaud and Light, 1992; Cairns et al., 1997; Yensen et al., 2002; Cairns et al., 2011; Pedersen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The decrease in force is paralleled by a decrease in the Ca2+ transient with depolarization of the resting potential beyond –60 mV.
source: The decrease in force is paralleled by a decrease in the Ca2+ transient with depolarization of the resting potential beyond –60 mV (Quiñonez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The decline in force is paralleled by reduction in extracellular recordings of compound muscle APs.
source: Consistent with this possibility, the decline in force is paralleled by reduction in extracellular recordings of compound muscle APs (Overgaard et al., 1999; Overgaard and Nielsen, 2001; Pedersen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Graded failure of excitation with depolarization of the resting potential manifests as either a gradual reduction in AP peak or as APs with variable amplitude that increase with increased current injection.
source: One possible explanation for this correlation is graded failure of excitation with depolarization of the resting potential, which manifests as either a gradual reduction in AP peak or as APs with variable amplitude that increase with increased current injection (Rich and Pinter, 2001; Rich and Pinter, 2003; Quiñonez et al., 2010; Ammar et al., 2015; Miranda et al., 2020; Uwera et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Reduction in AP peak can cause reduction in force generation.
source: Two studies have suggested that reduction in AP peak can cause reduction in force generation (Cairns et al., 2003; Gong et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Measurement of twitch force in the mouse extensor digitorum longus following elevation of extracellular K+ revealed an initial increase in force.
source: Measurement of twitch force in the mouse extensor digitorum longus (EDL) following elevation of extracellular K+ revealed an initial increase in force (Figure 1A, n = 3 muscles for each K+ concentration), which was followed by a decline that became faster with higher levels of extracellular K+ (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The initial increase in force following elevation of extracellular K+ was followed by a decline that became faster with higher levels of extracellular K+.
source: Measurement of twitch force in the mouse extensor digitorum longus (EDL) following elevation of extracellular K+ revealed an initial increase in force (Figure 1A, n = 3 muscles for each K+ concentration), which was followed by a decline that became faster with higher levels of extracellular K+ (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: With return to solution containing normal K+, force recovered rapidly.
source: With return to solution containing normal K+, force recovered rapidly.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: Between 10 and 14 mM K+, force went from near normal to almost 0 at 40 min after K+ infusion.
source: The K+ concentration dependence of force 40 min after K+ infusion was steep: between 10 and 14 mM, force went from near normal to almost 0 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In 10 mM K+, where force was near normal, Rm averaged –62.3 ± 1.0 mV.
source: in 10 mM K+, where force was near normal, Rm averaged –62.3 ± 1.0 mV (n = 5 mice, 50 fibers)
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: In 14 mM K+, where force had largely failed, Rm averaged –57.1 ± 1.5 mV.
source: in 14 mM K+, where force had largely failed it averaged –57.1 ± 1.5 mV (n = 4 mice, 32 fibers).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: A steep reduction of force is caused by depolarization over a narrow range of resting potentials.
source: These data suggest that a steep reduction of force is caused by depolarization over a narrow range of resting potentials (Figure 1B), similar to what has been reported previously (Cairns et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B and supported by a citation.

claim: AP amplitude decreased as the resting potential became more depolarized with elevation of extracellular K+.
source: AP amplitude decreased as the resting potential became more depolarized with elevation of extracellular K+ (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Small APs could still be triggered in many fibers at K+ concentrations (14 and 16 mM) at which force production was near 0.
source: What was somewhat surprising was that small APs could still be triggered in many fibers at K+ concentrations (14 and 16 mM) at which force production was near 0.
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation.

claim: Failure of force production is not due to failure to initiate APs.
source: These data suggest that failure of force production is not due to failure to initiate APs.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: GCAMP6f is a high-affinity Ca2+ indicator with a Kd near 600 nM in cardiomyocytes.
source: GCAMP6f is a high-affinity Ca2+ indicator with a Kd near 600 nM in cardiomyocytes such that it can detect changes in Ca2+ ranging from 100 nM to 5 µM (Shang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: GCAMP6f can detect changes in Ca2+ ranging from 100 nM to 5 µM.
source: GCAMP6f is a high-affinity Ca2+ indicator with a Kd near 600 nM in cardiomyocytes such that it can detect changes in Ca2+ ranging from 100 nM to 5 µM (Shang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Due to the high affinity of GCAMP6f it is not possible to study kinetics of the underlying Ca2+ signal.
source: However, due to the high affinity of GCAMP6f it is not possible to study kinetics of the underlying Ca2+ signal (Chen et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In normal extracellular K+, single APs generated a robust signal ΔF/F.
source: In normal extracellular K+, single APs generated a robust signal ΔF/F (Figure 3—video 1 associated with this submission).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: The normalized ΔF/F in 10 mM K+ was highly variable, both between fibers and muscles.
source: The normalized ΔF/F in 10 mM K+ was highly variable, both between fibers and muscles.
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation.

claim: The plot of ΔF/F versus resting potential was similar to the plot obtained for muscle force versus resting potential.
source: The plot of ΔF/F versus resting potential was similar to the plot obtained for muscle force versus resting potential (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference from comparing experimental data.

claim: Sudden failure to trigger Ca2+ release from the SR is the mechanism underlying the sudden depolarization-induced failure of ECC.
source: These data suggest that sudden failure to trigger Ca2+ release from the SR is the mechanism underlying the sudden depolarization-induced failure of ECC.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: When extracellular K+ was 3.5 mM, AP peak averaged +30 to +40 mV.
source: When extracellular K+ was 3.5 mM, AP peak averaged +30 to + 40 mV.
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: With elevation of K+ to 10, 12, 14, and 16 mM, AP peaks ranged from near +10 mV to –40 mV.
source: With elevation of K+ to 10, 12, 14, and 16 mM, AP peaks ranged from near +10 mV to –40 mV (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: When APs peak between –20 and –30 mV, small ΔF/F signals could be detected.
source: When APs peak between –20 and –30 mV, small ΔF/F signals could be detected and when APs peak below –30 mV, ΔF/F was 0 (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: When APs peak below –30 mV, ΔF/F was 0.
source: When APs peak between –20 and –30 mV, small ΔF/F signals could be detected and when APs peak below –30 mV, ΔF/F was 0 (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: Failure of the Ca2+ transient and force generation occurs prior to failure to initiate APs.
source: These data suggest that failure of the Ca2+ transient and force generation occurs prior to failure to initiate APs.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: When extracellular K+ was kept at 3.5 mM, the ΔF/F was stable over time, with a slight trend towards increasing.
source: When extracellular K+ was kept at 3.5 mM, the ΔF/F was stable over time, with a slight trend towards increasing (Figure 2A and B, 1.16 at 7 min vs. initial value normalized to 1, p=0.07, n = 5 fibers).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: With infusion of 16 mM K+, depolarization of the resting membrane potential was accompanied by graded reduction in the AP peak from a maximum ranging from +15 to +35 mV down to –25 to –45 mV.
source: With infusion of 16 mM K+, depolarization of the resting membrane potential was accompanied by graded reduction in the AP peak from a maximum ranging from +15 to + 35 mV down to –25 to –45 mV (Figure 2C, D and E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: The V50 for the resting potential at which AP peak was half maximal was –58.2 ± 3.3 mV.
source: The V50 for the resting potential at which AP peak was half maximal was –58.2 ± 3.3 mV, the slope factor k was 1.8 ± 0.6 mV, and the average value of the half-maximal AP peak at the V50 value was –15.5 ± 4.9 mV (n = 12 fibers from six mice).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement from Boltzmann fits.

claim: With depolarization during infusion of 16 mM K+, there was an initial increase in the ΔF/F from a mean normalized value of 0.81 ± 0.10 to the normalized maximum of 1.
source: With depolarization during infusion of 16 mM K+, there was an initial increase in the ΔF/F from a mean normalized value of 0.81 ± 0.10 to the normalized maximum of 1 (p<0.0001 paired t-test, n = 12, Figure 2D and F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: The initial increase in ΔF/F occurred despite reduction in AP peak.
source: This increase is similar to what has been reported previously (Quiñonez et al., 2010; Pedersen et al., 2019) and occurred despite reduction in AP peak (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation supported by citations.

claim: As depolarization progressed, there was rapid, complete loss of ΔF/F.
source: As depolarization progressed, there was rapid, complete loss of ΔF/F (Figure 2C, D and F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: The resting potential at which ΔF/F was half maximal was –57.5 ± 3.4 mV with a slope factor of 0.4 ± 0.2 mV.
source: The resting potential at which ΔF/F was half maximal was –57.5 ± 3.4 mV with a slope factor of 0.4 ± 0.2 mV (Figure 2F), which was significantly steeper than the slope for reduction in AP peak (p<1 × 10–5, paired t-test, n = 12 fibers from five mice).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement from Boltzmann fits with statistical analysis.

claim: The slope for reduction in ΔF/F with depolarization was significantly steeper than the slope for reduction in AP peak.
source: The resting potential at which ΔF/F was half maximal was –57.5 ± 3.4 mV with a slope factor of 0.4 ± 0.2 mV (Figure 2F), which was significantly steeper than the slope for reduction in AP peak (p<1 × 10–5, paired t-test, n = 12 fibers from five mice).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: The ΔF/F was half maximal at an AP peak of –21.0 ± 4.0 mV with a slope factor of 5.9 ± 1.7 mV.
source: The ΔF/F was half maximal at an AP peak of –21.0 ± 4.0 mV with a slope factor of 5.9 ± 1.7 mV.
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement from Boltzmann fits.

claim: The relationship between peak voltage and Ca2+ transient was within the range of values obtained from voltage-clamp studies of mouse muscle fibers.
source: This relationship between peak voltage and Ca2+ transient was within the range of values obtained from voltage-clamp studies of mouse muscle fibers (Wang et al., 1999; Ferreira Gregorio et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: APs peaking below –30 mV trigger little to no elevation of intracellular Ca2+ and hence generate little to no force.
source: These data suggest that APs peaking below –30 mV trigger little to no elevation of intracellular Ca2+ and hence generate little to no force.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: A loss of 11.6 ± 1.7 mV of resting potential was required to reduce AP amplitude from 90% to 10% of maximum.
source: A loss of 11.6 ± 1.7 mV of resting potential was required to reduce AP amplitude from 90% to 10% of maximum.
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: ΔF/F was reduced from 90% to 10% of maximum with a loss of only 4.1 ± 2.4 mV of resting potential.
source: In contrast, ΔF/F was reduced from 90% to 10% of maximum with a loss of only 4.1 ± 2.4 mV of resting potential (p<1 × 10–6 vs. APs, n = 12, paired Student's t-test).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement with statistical analysis.

claim: AP integral closely paralleled ΔF/F during depolarization of the resting potential.
source: AP integral closely paralleled ΔF/F during depolarization of the resting potential (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: When the normalized ΔF/F was plotted against normalized AP area, the mean R2 value was 0.86 ± 0.11.
source: When the normalized ΔF/F was plotted against normalized AP area, the mean R2 value was 0.86 ± 0.11 (Figure 3C, p<0.001 vs. the R2 value for ΔF/F vs. AP peak, n = 12 fibers, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement with statistical analysis.

claim: The R2 value for AP area vs. ΔF/F was significantly larger than the R2 value for AP peak vs. ΔF/F.
source: When the normalized ΔF/F was plotted against normalized AP area, the mean R2 value was 0.86 ± 0.11 (Figure 3C, p<0.001 vs. the R2 value for ΔF/F vs. AP peak, n = 12 fibers, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: The R2 value was larger for AP area vs. ΔF/F because AP area more closely mimicked the rapid decrease in ΔF/F.
source: The R2 value was larger for AP area vs. ΔF/F because AP area more closely mimicked the rapid decrease in ΔF/F (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The length constant of mouse EDL fibers is close to 0.5 mm.
source: The length constant of mouse EDL fibers is close to 0.5 mm (Riisager et al., 2014) such that depolarization due to passive spread of current from the current injecting electrode would be expected to be a minor contributor to depolarization of the membrane potential at the recording electrode.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Depolarization due to passive spread of current from the current injecting electrode would be expected to be a minor contributor to depolarization of the membrane potential at the recording electrode when electrodes are separated by 1.6 mm.
source: The length constant of mouse EDL fibers is close to 0.5 mm (Riisager et al., 2014) such that depolarization due to passive spread of current from the current injecting electrode would be expected to be a minor contributor to depolarization of the membrane potential at the recording electrode.
evidence: This is an inference based on the length constant measurement.

claim: Injection of 1000 nA of hyperpolarizing current for 0.2 ms caused no detectable voltage deflection at the recording electrode.
source: We confirmed that the 0.2 ms current injection used to trigger APs did not spread to the recording electrode: injection of 1000 nA of hyperpolarizing current for 0.2 ms caused no detectable voltage deflection (data not shown).
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation.

claim: With electrodes separated by 1.6 mm, two patterns of AP failure were observed: all or none failure with sudden drops in AP peak of 30–60 mV, and continuous reduction of AP peak.
source: With electrodes separated by 1.6 mm, we observed two patterns of AP failure. In some fibers, there was all or none failure, with sudden drops in AP peak of 30–60 mV (Figure 4B and E). In others, reduction of AP peak was continuous (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation.

claim: Reduction in AP peak was steeply dependent on resting potential, with a >40 mV reduction in peak occurring over 1–2 mV of resting potential.
source: Regardless of whether reduction in AP peak was sudden or continuous, it was steeply dependent on resting potential; with a >40 mV reduction in peak occurring over 1–2 mV of resting potential (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: The difference in resting potential between the last successful ECC and the first failed ECC was 0.8 ± 0.5 mV.
source: The difference in resting potential between the last successful ECC and the first failed ECC was 0.8 ± 0.5 mV (Figure 4G, n = 8 muscles).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: The AP peak of the last successful ECC averaged –12.8 ± 3.9 mV and by the first failed ECC it had dropped to –38.5 ± 6.3 mV.
source: The AP peak of the last successful ECC averaged –12.8 ± 3.9 mV and by the first failed ECC it had dropped to –38.5 ± 6.3 mV (Figure 4G, n = 8 muscles).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: The normalized integral of the last AP to successfully trigger ECC averaged 0.67 ± 0.12, and this fell to 0.03 ± 0.03 for the first failed ECC.
source: The normalized integral of the last AP to successfully trigger ECC averaged 0.67 ± 0.12, and this fell to 0.03 ± 0.03 for the first failed ECC.
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: The peaks of the last APs to trigger successful ECC along the length of the fiber ranged from –9.2 to –21.2 mV.
source: The peaks of the last APs to trigger successful ECC along the length of the fiber ranged from –9.2 to –21.2 mV (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: AP peak is as good as AP integral at predicting failure of conduction.
source: Neither measure has any overlap in values between successful and failed ECC. These data suggest that AP peak is as good as AP integral at predicting failure of conduction.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: At the time of failure of AP conduction, ΔF/F near the stimulating electrode still averaged 96% ± 15% of the ΔF/F at that ROI at a resting potential of –70 mV.
source: At the time of failure of AP conduction, ΔF/F near the stimulating electrode still averaged 96% ± 15% of the ΔF/F at that ROI at a resting potential of –70 mV (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: Local APs, which fail to conduct along the length of fibers, can be large enough to locally invade t-tubules, trigger gating of Cav1.1 channels and Ca2+ release from the SR.
source: These data suggest that local APs, which fail to conduct along the length of fibers, can be large enough to locally invade t-tubules, trigger gating of Cav1.1 channels and Ca2+ release from the SR.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: With electrodes close together, the average depolarization of resting potential between successful and failed AP conduction was only 0.5 ± 0.2 mV.
source: Similar to recordings with the electrodes far apart, the average depolarization of resting potential between successful and failed AP conduction was only 0.5 ± 0.2 mV (n = 10 muscles with 2–5 fibers, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: If APs peak above –21 mV, they conduct along the length of the fiber without decrement.
source: We conclude that, just like with electrodes far apart, AP peak is as good a predictor of AP conduction as AP integral. If APs peak above –21 mV, they conduct along the length of the fiber without decrement.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: APs peaking below –21 mV can trigger local Ca2+ release, but fail to conduct.
source: APs peaking below –21 mV can trigger local Ca2+ release, but fail to conduct.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The trigger for Ca2+ release from the SR is gating charge movement of Cav1.1 channels, which has a midpoint of inactivation of –57 mV.
source: The trigger for Ca2+ release from the SR is gating charge movement of Cav1.1 channels, which has a midpoint of inactivation of –57 mV (Ferreira Gregorio et al., 2017); a membrane potential at which ΔF/F sharply decreases.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mean 'AP' peak triggered by 5 ms current injection was 26.2 ± 6.3 mV and was triggered at a mean resting potential of –51.6 ± 4.6 mV.
source: The mean 'AP' peak triggered by 5 ms current injection was 26.2 ± 6.3 mV (n = 13 fibers from five muscles) and was triggered at a mean resting potential of –51.6 ± 4.6 mV.
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: The ΔF/F triggered by the artificial 'AP' averaged 92% ± 10% of the ΔF/F triggered by APs from the same fiber at a resting potential of –70 mV.
source: The ΔF/F triggered by the 'AP' averaged 92% ± 10% of the ΔF/F triggered by APs from the same fiber at a resting potential of –70 mV (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement.

claim: Following depolarization of the resting potential to –52 mV there is, at most, modest inactivation of SR Ca2+ release.
source: While these data do not rule out partial inactivation of SR Ca2+ release, they suggest that following depolarization of the resting potential to –52 mV there is, at most, modest inactivation of SR Ca2+ release.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Inactivation of Nav1.4, and the resultant failure of APs to sufficiently depolarize the fiber, is the primary mechanism underlying depolarization-induced failure of ECC.
source: We conclude that inactivation of Nav1.4, and the resultant failure of APs to sufficiently depolarize the fiber, is the primary mechanism underlying depolarization-induced failure of ECC.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Conduction velocity of mouse EDL muscle fibers has previously been measured using a three-electrode intracellular recording set up and by using a Ca2+ indicator dye.
source: Conduction velocity of mouse EDL muscle fibers has previously been measured using a three-electrode intracellular recording set up and by using a Ca2+ indicator dye (Riisager et al., 2014; Banks et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Declines in AP peak and AP area and the resultant failure to conduct along the length of muscle fibers were found during prolonged repetitive stimulation of fibers.
source: Declines in AP peak and AP area and the resultant failure to conduct along the length of muscle fibers were found during prolonged repetitive stimulation of fibers (Riisager et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Nonpropagating Ca2+ release triggered by depolarization at the end of fibers during bipolar extracellular stimulation has previously been demonstrated.
source: Nonpropagating Ca2+ release triggered by depolarization at the end of fibers during bipolar extracellular stimulation has also previously been demonstrated (Hernández-Ochoa et al., 2016; Banks et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: By –20 mV ~ 90% of all non-inactivated Na+ channels are activated in rat EDL.
source: Our previous loose patch voltage-clamp study in rat EDL revealed that by –20 mV ~ 90% of all non-inactivated Na+ channels are activated (Rich and Pinter, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Below –20 mV, there is a steep decline in the percentage of Na+ channels activated.
source: Below –20 mV, there is a steep decline in the percentage of Na+ channels activated.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of Na+ channels.

claim: Once APs peak below –21 mV any decrement in the peak as they conduct along the fiber lessens activation of Na+ channels and further reduces AP peak.

claim: AP peaks above –21 mV serve as a safety factor for ECC similar to the safety factor for synaptic transmission at the NMJ.
source: We conclude that AP peaks above –21 mV serve as a safety factor for ECC similar to the safety factor for synaptic transmission at the NMJ (Rich, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data with a citation for comparison.

claim: Conduction of APs along the length of fibers fails prior to failure of APs to conduct into t-tubules.
source: We propose that conduction of APs along the length of fibers fails prior to failure of APs to conduct into t-tubules.

claim: Ca2+ release from the SR begins to be triggered at voltages of –30 to –20 mV and becomes maximal at voltages above +10 mV.

claim: Depolarization of the resting potential triggers widening of APs.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Widening of APs contributes to the increase in Ca2+ signal that occurs following modest depolarization of the resting potential.

claim: The AP parameter responsible for propagation is the peak voltage.

claim: Movement of the Cav1.1 gating charges responsible for triggering opening of RyR1 and Ca2+ release from the SR is faster than opening of Cav1.1 channels.
source: Although movement of the Cav1.1 gating charges responsible for triggering opening of RyR1 and Ca2+ release from the SR is faster than opening of Cav1.1 channels, the movement of the gating charges in CaV1.1 is relatively slow compared to the upstroke of the AP (Schneider and Chandler, 1973; Banks et al., 2021; Savalli et al., 2021; Banks et al., 2022) such that the wider the AP, the greater the charge movement until saturation is reached.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.
